summary:
The Republic of Mordovia stands under the national framework of Russia, which applies in full and without identified local deviation. Russia presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes to official documents was signed; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that, explicitly, includes anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, detention of up to 15 days, and deportation, and national government warnings directed at LGBT travellers say so plainly.

The dedicated country dossier for Russia identified no deviation from the national position material enough to score separately (±0.02), so the Republic of Mordovia is assessed at the national score. For a trans traveller that position means same-sex marriage is banned, gender transition is banned, gender-marker changes on documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. Same-sex sexual activity as such is not criminalised.

Penalties are graded and severe. The 2013 propaganda law is punishable by administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days, escalating to up to four years' imprisonment on a repeat offence. Since the 2023 extremist designation, participation in the designated movement carries two to six years' imprisonment and organising it carries six to ten years.

Enforcement is active and documented. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions as of 30 June 2025 for alleged participation in the "International LGBT Movement" or for displaying its symbols, comprising about 98 administrative cases and 3 criminal cases. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged under article 282.2 who face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were convicted across 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols.

The volume of enforcement has risen alongside its severity. Cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding June 2025. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's extremist ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars: about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Detention carries lethal risk. In December 2024 a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. Physical coercion against transgender people is separately documented: a transgender woman was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping after police responded to a phone she had found.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) affirms the national legal position set out above and records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024.
tangentialFactors:
The Republic of Mordovia is one of Russia's constituent republics and generates no separate legal regime for transgender visitors; the national statutes, the Supreme Court designation and the administrative code articles cited above operate identically there. What varies across Russian territory is the intensity of enforcement activity, which in the capital has included coordinated overnight bar raids and mass searches, and no source in this inventory reports Mordovia-specific raids, prosecutions or official statements either way.

The trajectory of the national enforcement wave is the relevant comparison point for any Russian region. Human Rights Watch called on governments to offer safe haven to people fleeing Russia, and the UK Home Office note assesses that openly LGBT+ people face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution, with the state able but unwilling to protect. That assessment, not the absence of a local statute, is what a visitor in Mordovia would rely on if they sought protection after an incident.

Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, and a St Petersburg queer woman described herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation. The Moscow Times reported that picture of daily life alongside the legal position, which is the environment a visitor enters regardless of which federal subject they land in.

Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised anywhere in Russia, so the operative risk for a trans visitor is expression, documents and association rather than private conduct. The gap between that de jure position and the enforcement record — 101 convictions in under two years, eighteenfold growth in propaganda cases, and a death in pretrial detention — is the central turbulence in this dossier.
localsOnly:
Residents of the Republic of Mordovia live under the same prohibitions as visitors, but with no exit option framed as travel advice: gender-marker changes on documents are prohibited outright, gender transition is banned, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, so legal recognition and medical care are unavailable domestically rather than merely risky to seek.

The UK Home Office note records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024, and assesses that openly LGBT+ people face societal discrimination that may amount to persecution, with the state able but unwilling to protect. Under the Refugee Convention as applied by the UK, LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

Administrative exposure is routine rather than exceptional: article 20.3 cases for displaying banned symbols produced 98 administrative convictions, 81 of them individual, between January 2024 and June 2025, and propaganda-law fines generated more than 60 million rubles for the state budget over two years. Repeat propaganda offences are prosecuted criminally, carrying up to four years' imprisonment.

Coercive practices targeting transgender residents are documented outside formal care settings. A transgender woman was held for nine months from summer 2021 in a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour, and escaped only when police responded to a concealed phone.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory reports enforcement activity, official statements, healthcare availability or facilities specific to the Republic of Mordovia. The absence of Mordovia-specific reporting is unresolved rather than evidence of a more permissive local environment, and the national score is adopted because no regional deviation was identified, not because local practice has been independently verified.

The ±0.02 deviation figure cited for the dedicated country dossier is carried from the source inventory and has not been independently checked here; it records that no deviation material enough to score separately was found.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note is cited at version 2.0, June 2025, with a page update recorded on 12 August 2026. Whether a later revision alters the legal summary or the persecution assessment is unresolved against this inventory.

The inventory does not source current conditions for obtaining or renewing travel documents, entry or visa screening procedures that might expose a traveller's gender marker, or the practical availability of legal representation in Mordovia. Those points are not sourced and should not be read as cleared.
